name: Freud
line: Listen to what you did not mean to say.

quote.text: The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.
quote.source: The Interpretation of Dreams, chapter 7; sentence added in 1909, trans. James Strachey

quotes.text: Where id was, there ego shall be.
quotes.source: New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis, 1933, lecture 31, trans. James Strachey

quotes.text: The ego is not master in its own house.
quotes.source: A Difficulty in the Path of Psycho-Analysis, 1917, trans. James Strachey

quotes.text: Much will be gained if we succeed in transforming your hysterical misery into common unhappiness.
quotes.source: Studies on Hysteria, 1895, closing page, trans. James Strachey

quotes.text: He that has eyes to see and ears to hear may convince himself that no mortal can keep a secret. If his lips are silent, he chatters with his finger-tips; betrayal oozes out of him at every pore.
quotes.source: Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria, 1905, trans. James Strachey

quotes.text: The voice of the intellect is a soft one, but it does not rest till it has gained a hearing.
quotes.source: The Future of an Illusion, 1927, chapter 10, trans. James Strachey
His reported answer when asked what a normal person should be able to do well; told by Erik Erikson in Childhood and Society, 1950

words.usage: The part of the mind we have no direct access to. It holds wishes and memories that have been pushed out of awareness and go on acting.
The part of the mind that deals with reality and tries to reconcile the demands of the other two. The Latin word ego was the translator’s choice.
The oldest part: a cauldron of drives that knows no time, no contradiction and no no.
The internalised voice of parents and society. It watches, judges and punishes, often more harshly than they did.
A pressure from within the body that demands work of the mind. Often mistranslated as instinct.

words.meaning: The energy of the sexual drive
words.usage: For Freud, sexuality in a very wide sense: all the body’s seeking of pleasure and attachment, from infancy on.
Pushing an unacceptable wish or memory out of consciousness. What is repressed does not disappear. It returns in disguise.
The guardian of sleep, and the disguised fulfilment of a wish.
The title of his chief book. One works back from the dream as remembered to the thoughts behind it.
The mind’s nightly labour of turning hidden thoughts into a strange picture story.
What every dream attempts, by his account. A child’s dream shows the wish openly. An adult’s hides it.
Several thoughts fused into one dream image, as when a figure has one person’s face and another’s name.
Feeling shifted from what matters to something trivial, so that the important thing slips past the censor.
Slips of the tongue, forgotten names, mislaid keys. Strachey invented the word parapraxis for them.
Literally a free falling-in: whatever comes to mind. The patient undertakes to say it without selecting.
Everything in the patient that works against the cure: silences, lateness, changing the subject. Where it is strongest, something important lies.
Feelings that belong to early figures, carried over on to the analyst. At first an obstacle, then the main instrument of treatment.
Any of the mind’s ways of protecting itself from painful ideas: repression, denial, projection and others.
Turning a drive towards a higher, socially valued aim, such as art, science or care.
The tendency of the mind to seek pleasure and avoid unpleasure at once.
The learned ability to postpone pleasure in the light of how things actually are.
A small child’s love for one parent and rivalry with the other, and how it is resolved. He called it the kernel of the neuroses.
The tendency to re-enact a painful situation again and again without remembering its origin.
The slow labour by which an insight, once gained, is tested against resistance until it changes something.
The work of withdrawing one’s attachment, piece by piece, from someone or something lost.
The strangely familiar: something once known and long repressed that comes back.
A vivid, harmless childhood memory that stands in front of a more important one.
His late and most disputed idea: a tendency in living things towards rest, undoing and destruction, opposed by Eros.
The standing discomfort of living in civilisation, which demands that we give up part of our drives.
Jokes use the same tricks as dreams to let a forbidden thought through. He wrote a whole book on them.

practices.name: The dream book
practices.instructions: Keep a notebook and pen by the bed. On waking, before you move or speak, write down whatever you remember of your dreams, however broken or silly. Use the present tense. Then take the dream piece by piece. For each element, write what comes to mind, without judging. If nothing comes, write that. The rule of this Onda is to write down your dreams. This is a game of attention, not a diagnosis.
practices.why: Freud’s Interpretation of Dreams (1899) argued that dreams are meaningful. Writing them down is the one habit that lasts from his method.
variations: Draw one image from the dream.
Write the dream as a short story.
Tell it to a friend at breakfast.

practices.name: Catch a slip
practices.instructions: Carry a small card today. Each time you make a slip, write it down exactly: the wrong word said, the name that would not come, the thing mislaid, the appointment forgotten, the message sent to the wrong person. Do not explain it yet. In the evening look at the list. The rule of this Onda is to treat no slip as an accident.
practices.why: The Psychopathology of Everyday Life collects slips of the tongue and pen that Freud thought revealed hidden wishes. Even without his theory, collecting them is a good exercise in noticing.
variations: Note what you were thinking just before.
Share the funniest with a friend.

practices.name: The first thought
practices.instructions: The moment you wake, notice the very first thought that comes before you decide anything: a worry, a tune, a name, a task. Write it down in a word or a line. Don’t edit or interpret it. In a week, look at the list and see what recurs. Freud was interested in what the mind says when you are not looking.
practices.why: Attending to the first thought on waking is a form of free association. It catches the mind before the day’s self-presentation begins.
variations: Write the last thought of the night too.

practices.name: The weather in the body
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and ask where in your body this morning’s mood lives: tight shoulders, a heavy stomach, a restless leg, a clear chest. Write a line: today my mood is a ... in my ... Freud held that the ego is first of all a bodily ego. Noticing the body is the first step toward noticing yourself.
practices.why: The body is the first place where feeling shows. A weather report from inside gives the day a calmer start.
variations: Draw the feeling as a shape.

practices.name: Your earliest memory
practices.instructions: Write your earliest memory in as much detail as you can: where you were, what you saw, who was there, how it felt. Freud called such memories screen memories, because they often stand in front of something else. Do not search for the meaning. Just describe, and see what the memory is attached to.
practices.why: Deckerinnerungen, screen memories, are early memories that seem trivial but carry weight. Writing one out is a gentle way into your own history.
variations: Ask an older relative for theirs.

practices.name: Collect a joke
practices.instructions: Collect one joke today that made you laugh. Write it down. Then ask why it was funny. Freud wrote a whole book on jokes and the unconscious, holding that they release something we normally keep in check. Notice what the joke was about: authority, sex, stupidity, death. Tell it to someone.
practices.why: Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious (1905) is among Freud’s most readable books. Studying why a joke works is entertaining and revealing.
variations: Notice what you never laugh at.

practices.name: Free association
practices.instructions: Lie down where you will not be disturbed and where you cannot see a screen. Set a timer for fifteen minutes. Say aloud, or write without stopping, everything that passes through your mind, in the order it comes. Do not select, polish or censor. When you hit something you would rather not say, say it anyway, and note that you hesitated. The rule of this Onda is to say whatever comes to mind.
practices.why: Free association is the basic rule of psychoanalysis. As a solo writing exercise it can loosen thoughts you did not know you had.
variations: Say it into a voice recorder.

practices.name: Evenly hovering attention
practices.instructions: Ask someone how they are and then listen for twenty minutes. Give no advice and tell no story of your own. Do not try to remember anything in particular or to work anything out. Let your attention rest evenly on everything they say, and let your mind notice what stands out. Afterwards, write down what you noticed. The rule of this Onda is to listen more than you speak.
practices.why: Gleichschwebende Aufmerksamkeit, evenly hovering attention, was Freud’s way of listening. It is also a gift to anyone who wants to be heard.
variations: Do it with a family member.
Do it by phone with your eyes closed.
Notice when you want to interrupt.

practices.name: A city walk with open eyes
practices.instructions: Walk through a part of town you know, as Freud did after lunch, and look at it as a stranger would. Notice a shop sign you have never read, a building detail, a person’s gait. Pick one thing that surprises you and wonder why you never noticed it. Write down three things. Collecting small observations is how a mind learns.
practices.why: Freud took long walks in Vienna daily and said he found his best ideas on them. Looking freshly at the familiar is the heart of his method.
variations: Look up at the first floors.

practices.name: Turn the urge into a thing
practices.instructions: When an urge or irritation rises today, make something from it: a drawing, a poem, a tidy shelf, a fast walk, a pot of soup. Freud called this sublimation, the channelling of a drive into a creative or useful form. Spend twenty minutes making something with the energy you would otherwise spend fretting.
practices.why: Sublimierung is the Freudian name for turning drives into culture. It is a practical idea for anyone who gets restless.
variations: Write a furious letter you won’t send.

practices.name: Dig up an old object
practices.instructions: Choose an old object from a drawer or shelf: a toy, a letter, a photograph, a ticket. Hold it, look at it and tell its story aloud. Ask what it meant, what it still means and why you kept it. Freud filled his rooms with ancient figures and compared the mind to a buried city. Put it back or let it go.
practices.why: Freud’s collection of antiquities surrounded him as he worked, and he compared analysis to archaeology. Handling an old object is a small dig.

practices.name: Say the unsaid kind thing
practices.instructions: Say aloud to someone a thing you have been thinking but not saying, something kind: I appreciate you, I have missed you, you helped me more than you know. Unspoken gratitude is a kind of repression, and its release is a pleasure. Choose someone near and say it plainly. Notice your hesitation first.
practices.why: Freud held that what is held back builds pressure. Saying the kind unsaid thing is a pleasant way to let some off.
variations: Say it to someone who has died, in a letter.

practices.name: What am I repeating?
practices.instructions: Think of something that went wrong today between you and another person, or within you. Now look back for the same shape earlier in your life: the same kind of quarrel, the same disappointment, the same way of leaving. Write the chain in a few lines. You are not looking for blame, only for the pattern. Wiederholungszwang, the compulsion to repeat, can be loosened by being seen.
practices.why: Freud observed that we tend to repeat the unresolved. Spotting a pattern is the first step towards choice. The rule of this Onda is to look for the repetition.
variations: Look at one pattern per week.
Ask a friend if they see the same one.

practices.name: Ask the night a question
practices.instructions: Before sleep, write down one question you would like your dreams to bear on: What do I want? Why am I tired? What am I avoiding? Leave it by the bed with the pen. In the morning, see whether your dream book has anything to say. You may find that it answers more than you expected, or nothing at all, which is also information.
practices.why: Dream incubation is an ancient practice: posing a question before sleep. It goes well with a dream book and costs nothing.
variations: Ask a question about a decision.

practices.name: An hour in a café
practices.instructions: Spend an hour in a café, ideally an old-fashioned one with marble tables and newspapers, as Freud did at the Landtmann. Order a coffee, sit with it and watch people. Read, write, or listen. Let your mind drift. If no café is near, make a pot of coffee at home and set a good table. The coffeehouse is Vienna’s living room.
practices.why: Café Landtmann was Freud’s favourite coffeehouse, and Viennese cafés are made for slow thought. An hour there is a ritual of its own.

practices.name: Listen to the Adagietto
practices.instructions: Play the Adagietto from Mahler’s Fifth Symphony, written in Vienna in 1901, a slow, intimate piece for strings and harp. Sit in the dark and notice what it stirs: a memory, an image, a longing. Mahler consulted Freud in 1910, famously for an afternoon’s walk in the Dutch city of Leiden. Let the music be your free association.
practices.why: Mahler and Freud walked and talked through Leiden for four hours in 1910. The Adagietto is Mahler at his most direct.
variations: Listen with a closed notebook beside you.
Write what came to mind afterwards.

practices.name: A hand of cards
practices.instructions: Play a game of cards with friends or family, ideally a trick-taking game such as tarock, whist or skat. Freud played tarock every Saturday evening with his friends for decades. Chat during the hands, and notice who bluffs and who plays safe. Games are a good place to observe the self at work. Keep stakes to nothing.
practices.why: Freud’s weekly tarock evening was his one fixed pleasure, kept for decades. A card game is also a quiet laboratory of character.
variations: Learn the rules of a Viennese game.

practices.name: Spot the uncanny
practices.instructions: At dusk, take a short walk and look for the uncanny, das Unheimliche: something familiar that has become strange. A shop dummy, a doorway in the half-light, your own reflection in a window, a doll. Note what gives you the shiver, and why. Freud wrote an essay on it, linking it to the return of the half-forgotten. Enjoy the mild thrill and go home.
practices.why: Das Unheimliche (1919) is Freud’s essay on why the familiar can become eerie. Looking for it at dusk is a fun, safe way to meet the idea.
variations: Read the first page of the essay.
Tell a ghost story to a friend.

practices.name: A Viennese coffeehouse afternoon
practices.instructions: Spend an afternoon in a coffeehouse, real or imagined. Order a melange or a small black coffee with a glass of water, then read the paper, write postcards, play chess, argue with a friend and watch the room. Stay for two hours without being hurried. The Viennese coffeehouse was where half of modern thought was talked into being. Tip generously.
practices.why: Vienna’s coffeehouses were open study halls of the city. An afternoon in one, with no rush, is a unique pleasure.
variations: Meet a friend and talk freely.

practices.name: A summer walk and talk
practices.instructions: Take a long walk in the woods or hills with a friend, as Freud did in the mountains each summer. Talk about whatever comes: childhood, dreams, plans, fears. Stop for a rest and a snack. Do not try to solve anything. Pick wild strawberries or flowers only if you know them well. Keep to paths, and tell someone where you are going.
practices.why: Freud spent every summer walking in the Alps, where he did some of his best thinking. A day of it is a holiday for the mind.
variations: Walk in silence for the first half hour.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Interpretation of Dreams
immersePlan.text: Read the opening of Freud’s great book, with the dream of Irma’s injection, or any chapter. Compare it with your own dream notes.

immersePlan.name: Read about slips in everyday life
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Freud’s book of forgotten names, misread words and slips of the tongue. Notice how funny many of them are.

immersePlan.name: Read the Five Lectures
immersePlan.text: Read the first of the lectures Freud gave at Clark University in 1909 for a general audience. It is the clearest short introduction.

immersePlan.name: Watch Spellbound
immersePlan.text: Watch Hitchcock’s 1945 thriller with Ingrid Bergman as a psychoanalyst, featuring a dream sequence designed by Salvador Dalí. Notice the dream.

immersePlan.name: Watch A Dangerous Method
immersePlan.text: Watch David Cronenberg’s 2011 film about the friendship and split between Freud and Jung, with Viggo Mortensen as Freud. Notice the debates.

immersePlan.name: Watch Freud’s Last Session
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2023 film in which Freud, dying in London, argues with C. S. Lewis about God. Notice how the two men listen.

immersePlan.name: Listen to The Marriage of Figaro
immersePlan.text: Play the overture and a few arias from Mozart’s opera, about servants outwitting their master. Freud loved Mozart’s operas.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Mahler Adagietto
immersePlan.text: Play the slow movement for strings and harp, written in Vienna in 1901. Close your eyes and note the images that arise.

immersePlan.name: Hear Freud’s voice
immersePlan.text: Play the 1938 BBC recording of Freud himself, aged eighty-two, speaking in English after fleeing Vienna. Listen to his dry humour.

immersePlan.name: Look at Freud’s couch
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the couch with its Persian rug and cushions, now in the Freud Museum in London. Think about the hours spent there.

immersePlan.name: Look at Freud’s antiquities
immersePlan.text: Look at the Egyptian, Greek and Roman figures that crowded his desk. Pick one and imagine what it said to him.

immersePlan.name: Look at Michelangelo’s Moses
immersePlan.text: Look at Michelangelo’s marble Moses, which Freud visited every day for three weeks and wrote about. Look at the stance and the beard.

immersePlan.name: Cook tafelspitz
immersePlan.text: Simmer beef with root vegetables in a good broth, and serve with horseradish and apple. It is Vienna’s Sunday dish and Freud’s favourite.

immersePlan.name: Make or eat apfelstrudel
immersePlan.text: Bake or buy a slice of apple strudel, with thin pastry rolled around spiced apples. Eat it with coffee.

immersePlan.name: Cook shop-bought mushrooms
immersePlan.text: Fry mushrooms in butter with parsley, as Freud loved to when he went mushroom hunting. Use only mushrooms bought from a shop or market; never eat wild ones unless an expert has identified them.

immersePlan.name: Make a melange
immersePlan.text: Make strong coffee and top it with steamed milk and a spoon of foam. It is the Viennese cappuccino.

immersePlan.name: Drink black coffee after lunch
immersePlan.text: Drink a small, strong black coffee after lunch, slowly, with a glass of water.

immersePlan.name: Drink mineral water
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of mineral water, as Freud did at the spa town of Karlsbad. Notice the taste.

immersePlan.name: Take a fifty-five-minute hour
immersePlan.text: Give a task or a person a fixed fifty-five minutes of uninterrupted attention, as in an analytic hour. Stop on time.

immersePlan.name: Hold a Wednesday meeting
immersePlan.text: Gather two or three friends for an evening of free-ranging conversation on one idea, with coffee and cake, in the spirit of Freud’s Wednesday group.

immersePlan.name: Plan a mountain summer day
immersePlan.text: Plan a day of walking in hills or woods, as Freud did each summer. Choose a route and a day.

immersePlan.name: Play tarock
immersePlan.text: Play a trick-taking game, tarock if you can learn it, or any similar. Freud played every Saturday.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of chess
immersePlan.text: Play a game of chess and notice your own style, careful or reckless. Talk about it afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Learn about mushroom hunting
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of edible mushrooms in a field guide, or visit a market. Never eat a wild mushroom you cannot identify with an expert.

immersePlan.name: Keep Freud’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Freud was born on 6 May 1856. Keep a dream notebook for a week in his honour.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Sigmund Freud Museum
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Berggasse 19 in Vienna, where Freud lived and worked for nearly fifty years. Imagine the waiting room.

immersePlan.name: Look up Café Landtmann
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Freud’s favourite Vienna café. Imagine his table.

immersePlan.name: Practise Freier Einfall
immersePlan.text: Freier Einfall is free association. Write for five minutes without stopping, whatever comes to mind.

immersePlan.name: Practise Fehlleistung
immersePlan.text: Fehlleistung is a slip, a faulty act. Notice one slip today and write it down without explanation.

immersePlan.name: Practise Witz
immersePlan.text: Witz is a joke or wit. Tell one joke today and think about why it works.

rules.why: Before anything else in the morning. They are the plainest report you will get from the part of you that you do not hear.
For a set time each day, do not censor. What you most want to leave out matters most.

rules.text: Treat no slip as an accident
rules.why: Ask what a forgetting or a wrong word might have been for.
Give others even, patient attention. Offer no advice until you have understood.
When the same trouble returns, stop blaming the occasion and study the pattern.

rules.text: Be honest with yourself above all
rules.why: Do not prettify your motives. Self-knowledge begins where it is unflattering.

read.title: The Interpretation of Dreams
read.creator: Sigmund Freud, trans. Joyce Crick or James Strachey
read.why: The founding book. Full of his own dreams, including the one about his patient Irma on which the method was first tried.

read.title: The Psychopathology of Everyday Life
read.creator: Sigmund Freud
read.why: Slips of the tongue, forgotten names and bungled actions. His most entertaining book and an easy way in.

read.title: Five Lectures on Psycho-Analysis
read.creator: Sigmund Freud
read.why: The talks he gave in America in 1909. The whole theory in fifty clear pages.

read.title: Civilization and Its Discontents
read.creator: Sigmund Freud
read.why: Why we are unhappy in the societies we build to protect us. Short, dark and written on the eve of catastrophe.

read.title: Freud: A Life for Our Time
read.creator: Peter Gay
read.why: The standard biography by a historian who admired him without being blind.

read.title: Becoming Freud
read.creator: Adam Phillips
read.why: A psychoanalyst’s short book about the first fifty years and about how unreliable any life story is.

watch.title: A Dangerous Method
watch.creator: David Cronenberg
watch.why: The friendship and rupture between Freud and Jung, and the patient who became an analyst. Careful and close to the letters.

watch.title: Freud
watch.creator: John Huston
watch.why: Montgomery Clift as the young doctor finding his way to the unconscious. Sombre and of its time, with striking dream scenes.

watch.title: Spellbound
watch.creator: Alfred Hitchcock
watch.why: A thriller solved by dream interpretation, with a dream sequence designed by Salvador Dalí.

watch.title: Freud’s Last Session
watch.creator: Matt Brown
watch.why: An imagined meeting between the dying Freud and C. S. Lewis in London in September 1939.

listen.title: The Marriage of Figaro
listen.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
listen.why: Freud claimed to be unmusical, but he loved this opera and Don Giovanni and quoted them often.

listen.title: Symphony No. 5, Adagietto
listen.creator: Gustav Mahler
listen.why: In 1910 Mahler, in despair over his marriage, walked for four hours with Freud through the Dutch town of Leiden. It was a single session and seems to have helped.

listen.title: Erwartung
listen.creator: Arnold Schoenberg, libretto by Marie Pappenheim
listen.why: A woman searches a forest at night for her lover. Half an hour of music from Freud’s Vienna that sounds like the inside of an anxious mind.

listen.title: Sigmund Freud speaks
listen.creator: BBC recording
listen.why: The only known recording of his voice: two minutes in English, made in London, summing up his life’s work.

art.title: The couch
art.creator: With its Persian rug and cushions
art.why: A gift from a grateful patient. He covered it with a Qashqai carpet and sat in a green armchair behind its head. In the Freud Museum, London.

art.title: His collection of antiquities
art.creator: Egyptian, Greek, Roman and Chinese
art.why: More than two thousand small figures crowded his desk and shelves. He compared analysis to archaeology: digging down through layers.

art.title: Moses
art.creator: Michelangelo
art.why: The seated prophet in San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome. Freud visited daily for three weeks in 1913 and published an essay on what the statue is doing with its hands.

art.title: Portrait of Sigmund Freud
art.creator: Salvador Dalí
art.why: Dalí sketched him during a visit in London. Freud remarked that in classic paintings he looked for the unconscious, and in Surrealist ones for the conscious.

eat.title: Tafelspitz
eat.creator: Beef simmered with root vegetables, served with horseradish and chive sauce
eat.why: The great dish of Vienna, and the main meal of the day in the Freud household, served at one o’clock sharp.

eat.title: Wild mushrooms
eat.creator: Fried in butter with parsley
eat.why: He was a passionate mushroom hunter on his summer holidays and led his children through the woods to find them.

eat.title: Artichokes
eat.creator: Boiled, with butter
eat.why: His favourite vegetable. He disliked cauliflower and would not eat chicken.

eat.title: Apfelstrudel
eat.creator: Thin pastry rolled round apples, raisins and cinnamon
eat.why: The coffee house sweet. Order it at the Landtmann.

drink.title: A melange
drink.creator: Viennese coffee with steamed milk
drink.why: Taken at the Café Landtmann on the Ring, his usual coffee house, with the newspapers.

drink.title: Spa water
drink.creator: Mineral water from Karlsbad
drink.why: He took the cure there several summers for his digestion.

customs.title: The analytic hour
customs.creator: Fifty-five minutes, the same time each day
customs.why: Patients came six days a week. He saw eight or more a day, then wrote from nine until past midnight.

customs.title: Behind the couch
customs.creator: Out of the patient’s sight
customs.why: The patient lies down and looks at nothing. He said he could not bear being stared at for eight hours a day, and that it kept his own expression from interfering.

customs.title: The Wednesday meetings
customs.creator: From 1902
customs.why: A few doctors met in his waiting room each week with coffee and cake to discuss cases. It became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society.

customs.title: Summer in the mountains
customs.creator: Three months of walking and writing
customs.why: Each year the family left Vienna for the Alps. Several of his books were drafted there.

games.title: Tarock
games.creator: Card game · Austria
games.why: A trick-taking game played with tarot cards. Freud played every Saturday evening with the same friends for decades and would not miss it.

games.title: Chess
games.creator: Board game
games.why: He played in coffee houses as a young man, and compared learning analysis to learning chess: only the openings and endgames can be taught.

games.title: Mushroom hunting
games.creator: Outdoor pursuit · Austria
games.why: A family contest in the woods. On finding a fine specimen he would throw his hat over it and blow a silver whistle to call the others.

festivals.title: Freud’s birthday
festivals.creator: 6 May
festivals.why: Born in 1856. The Sigmund Freud Lecture is given in Vienna each year on or near this day.

festivals.title: The Long Night of Museums
festivals.creator: The first Saturday of October, across Austria
festivals.why: One ticket opens hundreds of museums until after midnight, the house at Berggasse 19 among them.

festivals.title: Congress of the International Psychoanalytical Association
festivals.creator: Every two years, in summer
festivals.why: The meeting of the body Freud founded in 1910. The first congress was held at Salzburg in 1908.

places.title: Sigmund Freud Museum
places.creator: Berggasse 19, Vienna, Austria
places.why: The apartment and consulting rooms where he lived and worked for forty-seven years. The rooms are nearly empty, because he took almost everything with him in 1938, and the emptiness is part of the exhibit.

places.title: Freud Museum London
places.creator: 20 Maresfield Gardens, Hampstead, London, United Kingdom
places.why: The house of his last year, where the study was set up exactly as in Vienna. The couch, the desk and the antiquities are all here.

places.title: Café Landtmann
places.creator: Universitätsring 4, Vienna, Austria
places.why: The grand coffee house beside the Burgtheater where he read the papers. Still in business.

places.title: Bellevue
places.creator: Himmelstrasse, Vienna, Austria
places.why: A hillside above the city. A stone tablet marks where, on 24 July 1895, the secret of dreams revealed itself to him, as he joked in a letter.

places.title: Freud’s birthplace
places.creator: Příbor, Czech Republic
places.why: The small house in Moravia where he was born in a rented room above a blacksmith. Now a museum.

ethics.title: Honesty with oneself
ethics.text: The whole method rests on not turning away from what one finds. He called analysis an education in truthfulness.
ethics.practice: Admit to yourself one motive today that does not flatter you.

ethics.title: Patience
ethics.text: Minds change slowly. Insight has to be worked through many times before it holds.
ethics.practice: Take up again something you have already understood but not yet changed.

ethics.title: Abstaining from judgment
ethics.text: The analyst listens without praise or blame so that everything can be said.
ethics.practice: Hear one confession today, your own or another’s, without verdict.

ethics.title: Love and work
ethics.text: A person is well when they can do both. Neither needs to be grand.
ethics.practice: Give honest effort to one piece of work and real attention to one person.

ethics.title: Bearing reality
ethics.text: Maturity is giving up comforting illusions and still finding life worth living.
ethics.practice: Name one wishful belief you hold, and look at the facts.

ethics.title: Humour
ethics.text: A joke lets the truth out and spares us pain. He prized it, and kept it through sixteen years of cancer.
ethics.practice: Find the joke in something that shamed you.

philosophy.title: The unconscious
philosophy.text: Most of mental life goes on outside awareness, and it has purposes of its own. Consciousness is the tip.
philosophy.practice: Recall a decision you explained with good reasons. What else might have decided it?

philosophy.title: Dreams as wishes
philosophy.text: A dream stages the fulfilment of a wish, disguised so that it will not wake us.
philosophy.practice: Take last night’s dream and ask what it gave you that the day refused.

philosophy.title: Nothing is accidental
philosophy.text: Slips, forgettings and symptoms have meaning. The mind does not do things at random.
philosophy.practice: Take today’s smallest mistake seriously for two minutes.

philosophy.title: Id, ego and superego
philosophy.text: We are not one. The I serves three masters: the drives, the conscience and the outside world.
philosophy.practice: In one inner conflict today, sort out which voice is which.

philosophy.title: Childhood persists
philosophy.text: The earliest loves and fears set the patterns we follow as adults. The child is still there.
philosophy.practice: Whose approval were you seeking today, really?

philosophy.title: Transference
philosophy.text: We meet new people as if they were old ones. Strong feelings towards a stranger are often a letter addressed to someone else.
philosophy.practice: Who does the person who irritates you most remind you of?

philosophy.title: Civilisation and its cost
philosophy.text: Living together requires us to hold back aggression and desire. The price is guilt and a permanent unease.
philosophy.practice: What did you give up today for the sake of getting along?

philosophy.title: Mourning
philosophy.text: Loss is worked through piece by piece. Grief is not an illness. Refusing to grieve can become one.
philosophy.practice: What have you lost that you have not yet let yourself miss?

journal: What did you not want to write down today?
What did you dream, and what was the wish?
What did you forget, and whom did that suit?
What slipped out?
Where did you fall silent?
What are you repeating?
Whose voice does your conscience speak in?
Who did someone remind you of today?
What feeling was too big for its occasion?
What did you want as a child that you still want?
What do you find hardest to say aloud?
What are you guilty about, and is the guilt earned?
What did you laugh at, and what was the joke hiding?
Whom do you envy?

What have you not mourned?
Which of your reasons today was a cover?
What made you anxious, and what was the danger?
Where did you obey a rule nobody is enforcing?
What would you do if you were not afraid of what you might want?
What did you turn into work today that began as something else?
Whom did you really listen to?
What childhood scene keeps coming back, and what stands behind it?
What do you want from your parents still?
What comforting belief are you holding on to?
When did you feel uncanny?

reflect: What did your dreams keep returning to?
Which slips turned out to mean something?
What pattern have you seen often enough to believe?
Whom do you hear differently now?
What will you go on working through?

intro: Sigmund Freud was born in 1856 in a small Moravian town, the eldest son of a Jewish wool merchant, and brought to Vienna at the age of three. He was the pride of the family, read eight languages, and trained as a doctor and a researcher on the nervous system. He would have preferred a life in the laboratory, but he was poor, Jewish in an antisemitic university, and wanted to marry. In 1886 he opened a private practice for nervous diseases.

His patients were mostly women with symptoms that had no bodily cause: paralyses, coughs, lost voices, terrors. Medicine called it hysteria and had little to offer. Freud had seen the great Charcot in Paris produce and remove such symptoms by hypnosis, and an older Viennese colleague, Josef Breuer, had told him of a patient whose symptoms vanished one by one as she talked her way back to the moments when they first appeared. She called it her talking cure. Freud took the hint further than Breuer wished to go.

He gave up hypnosis and asked his patients simply to lie down and say whatever came into their heads. What he heard, and what he found when he turned the same method on his own dreams after his father’s death, convinced him of several things. Much of the mind is unconscious. Painful wishes and memories are actively pushed out of awareness, and return as symptoms, dreams, slips and jokes. These wishes are very often sexual in a broad sense and go back to early childhood. And patients re-live their oldest relationships with the doctor, which makes it possible to understand and loosen them.

He set this out in The Interpretation of Dreams, published at the end of 1899. It sold 351 copies in six years. But a circle gathered round him on Wednesday evenings, the movement spread to Zurich, Budapest, Berlin, London and New York, and by the 1920s his vocabulary had entered ordinary speech. He kept revising. After the First World War he added the model of id, ego and superego, and a drive towards destruction alongside the drive to love. In his last decade he wrote about religion and civilisation with a calm pessimism.

In 1923 he was found to have cancer of the jaw, the result of twenty cigars a day. He underwent more than thirty operations and worked on. When Germany annexed Austria in 1938 the Gestapo searched his home and questioned his daughter Anna. Friends and a ransom got him to London, where he died in September 1939. Four of his sisters were murdered in the camps.

Freud’s claims to have founded a science have not held up well, and much of his theory has been revised or dropped. What has lasted is a way of paying attention: the idea that people mean more than they know, that listening without judgment lets it emerge, and that self-knowledge is slow, unflattering and worth it. This Onda borrows that attention. It is a set of exercises in noticing. It is not therapy and does not replace it.
guide.origin: Vienna, capital of the Habsburg empire, in a second-floor flat at Berggasse 19
guide.era: Freud was born in 1856, founded psychoanalysis in the 1890s and died in exile in London in 1939

figures.name: Sigmund Freud
figures.bio: Neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis. A prodigious worker, a fine German stylist and a devoted, old-fashioned family man.

figures.name: Josef Breuer
figures.bio: A distinguished Viennese physician, Freud’s early patron and co-author of Studies on Hysteria. He drew back from the emphasis on sexuality.

figures.name: Bertha Pappenheim
figures.bio: Breuer’s patient, known as Anna O., who invented the phrase talking cure. She later became a pioneering social worker and feminist.

figures.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
figures.bio: The Paris neurologist whose demonstrations of hysteria under hypnosis showed the young Freud that ideas can cause bodily symptoms.

figures.name: Wilhelm Fliess
figures.bio: A Berlin ear, nose and throat doctor and Freud’s closest confidant in the 1890s. The letters to him record the birth of psychoanalysis.

figures.name: Martha Freud
figures.bio: Born Martha Bernays. They were engaged for four years and exchanged some fifteen hundred letters. She ran the household that made his working day possible.

figures.name: Carl Gustav Jung
figures.bio: The Swiss psychiatrist Freud chose as his heir. They broke in 1913 over the nature of the libido and of the unconscious.

figures.name: Anna Freud
figures.bio: His youngest child, analysed by him, his nurse and companion in illness. She founded child psychoanalysis and the study of the ego’s defences.

figures.name: Lou Andreas-Salomé
figures.bio: Writer and former friend of Nietzsche and Rilke who became an analyst in her fifties and one of Freud’s most valued correspondents.

figures.name: Marie Bonaparte
figures.bio: A princess of Greece and Denmark, his patient and friend. She paid the tax the Nazis demanded for his release and saved his letters to Fliess.

history.detail: Now Příbor in the Czech Republic. The family moves to Vienna in 1860 after his father’s business fails.
A travel grant takes him to Charcot at the Salpêtrière hospital. He returns to Vienna, marries and opens his practice.
The family moves into the flat where he will live and work until 1938.
Written with Breuer. On 24 July, at the Bellevue above Vienna, he analyses his own dream of Irma’s injection.
His father dies. He begins to analyse his own dreams and memories and gives up his theory that every neurosis goes back to an actual seduction in childhood.
The publisher dates it 1900. The Psychopathology of Everyday Life follows in 1901.
Four colleagues begin meeting weekly in his waiting room. Within a decade there are societies in six countries.
He publishes his theory of sexuality and the case of an eighteen-year-old who walked out of treatment, from whom he learned about transference.
He lectures at Clark University in Massachusetts with Jung and Ferenczi. It is his only visit and brings his first honorary degree.
After years of growing strain the friendship ends. A secret committee of loyal followers is formed to guard the movement.
Beyond the Pleasure Principle introduces the death drive, months after his daughter Sophie dies of influenza. The Ego and the Id sets out the three agencies. His cancer is diagnosed.
He receives the Goethe Prize for literature. Three years later his books are burned in Berlin.
He leaves Vienna on 4 June 1938 by the Orient Express. He dies in Hampstead on 23 September 1939, three weeks into the war, at his own request by an overdose of morphine from his doctor.

concepts.text: The larger part of the mind.
concepts.detail: Not merely what we are unaware of at a given moment. It is what is kept from awareness by force, and it follows its own rules, with no sense of time or contradiction.
The cornerstone of the theory. An idea that would cause too much distress is denied entry to consciousness, and uses up energy to keep there.

concepts.text: From latent thoughts to manifest dream.
concepts.detail: Condensation, displacement, the turning of thoughts into pictures, and a final tidying into a story. Interpretation runs the process backwards.
The patient says whatever occurs to them. The analyst listens for the threads that connect what seems unconnected.
The patient comes to feel towards the analyst what they once felt towards parents and others. Analysing this is the core of the treatment.
Children seek bodily pleasure and form passionate attachments long before puberty. The idea scandalised his contemporaries more than any other.
Introduced in 1923. The id presses for satisfaction, the superego forbids and demands, and the ego mediates between them and the world.
One binds things together into larger unities. The other seeks to undo and return to rest. Human life is their conflict and alloy.
The redirection of drives to non-sexual, valued aims. Art, science and civilisation itself are built on it, at some cost in happiness.

facts.text: The first edition of The Interpretation of Dreams was six hundred copies. It took eight years to sell them.
Freud was nominated for the Nobel Prize in medicine thirty-two times and for literature once, and never won.
He saw his first patients of the day at eight and worked until one, then again from three until nine in the evening.
His dog, a chow called Jofi, sat in on sessions. He said she always knew when the hour was up.
The English words ego, id, cathexis and parapraxis are his translator’s Latin and Greek. Freud wrote in plain German: the I, the it.
His ashes rest in an ancient Greek urn from his own collection, at Golders Green in London.

sensitivity.note: This Onda borrows Freud’s habits of attention: recording dreams, speaking freely, noticing slips and listening. It is not psychoanalysis and it is not treatment. If you are struggling, please see a doctor or a qualified therapist.
requiredCaveats: The scientific standing of Freud’s theories is contested, and many specific claims have been abandoned. They are presented here as his ideas, not as established fact.
His views on women and on sexuality reflect his time and have been strongly and rightly criticised, not least by later analysts.
Free association and dream work can bring up painful material. Go gently, and stop if it becomes too much.
Freud’s cigars killed him, and his early enthusiasm for cocaine harmed a friend. Neither is part of this Onda.
